title: Star clusters
subtitle: Young loose families and ancient crowded swarms: the best deep-sky targets for a city and a pair of binoculars.

sections.heading: Open clusters: young families
body: After this lesson you will be able to tell the two kinds of star cluster apart, find the best examples of each, and explain why five stars of the Big Dipper belong together.

Stars are born in batches. When a nebula has finished forming stars, what remains is an open cluster: a loose group of a few dozen to a few thousand stars, all the same age, drifting together through the disc of the Milky Way. Open clusters are young by stellar standards, typically tens to hundreds of millions of years old, and they slowly dissolve as their stars wander off.

The finest is [[dso:M45|the Pleiades]], a tiny dipper of blue-white stars about 440 light-years away and around 100 million years old. Beside it, the V of the Bull's face is [[dso:C41|the Hyades]], the nearest open cluster of all at about 150 light-years. (Bright orange [[star:Aldebaran|Aldebaran]] is not a member; it lies less than half as far away, in the same line of sight.) Others to learn: [[dso:M44|the Beehive]] in Cancer, [[dso:C14|the Double Cluster]] between Perseus and Cassiopeia, and [[dso:M7|M7]] near the Scorpion's sting.

steps.caption: Taurus holds the two nearest bright open clusters: the tight knot of the Pleiades and the wide V of the Hyades. Aldebaran only appears to be part of the V.
The Double Cluster lies halfway between the W of Cassiopeia and the top of Perseus: two open clusters side by side, about 7,500 light-years away.
The Beehive sits in the middle of dim Cancer, between Pollux and Regulus. The circle shows a typical 5° binocular field; the cluster fits comfortably inside.

figures.caption: Open clusters are loose families of stars born together. Each looks different because each is a different age: the Pleiades still has hot blue stars, the older Beehive has lost them, and the Double Cluster is a pair of very young clusters.

All the stars in a cluster are the same age, so a cluster ages as a whole. Slide the age: the heaviest, bluest stars die first, so a cluster’s light turns from blue-white to yellow over billions of years. Jump to real clusters to see where they stand.

thinkAbout.question: The Pleiades contains bright blue B stars, but no O stars at all. What does that tell you about its age?
thinkAbout.answer: It is older than an O star’s whole lifetime of a few million years, yet younger than a bright B star’s lifetime of a few hundred million. Any O stars it was born with have already died; the clock that tells a cluster’s age is which of its heaviest stars are still shining.

sections.tryIt: Count the Pleiades. Most people see six stars by eye; from the city you may get four or five. Then use binoculars: dozens appear, and the whole cluster fits in one view.

sections.heading: Globular clusters: ancient swarms
body: Globular clusters are a different thing altogether: tight balls of hundreds of thousands of stars, packed so densely that the center blurs into a solid glow. They are among the oldest objects known, 11 to 13 billion years old, nearly as old as the universe. Instead of lying in the Milky Way's disc, the galaxy's 150 or so globulars swarm around its center in a great sphere called the halo, which is why so many are found toward Sagittarius, Scorpius and Ophiuchus.

The best for northern observers is [[dso:M13|M13]] in Hercules, on one side of the Keystone, about 22,000 light-years away. [[dso:M22|M22]] near the lid of the Sagittarius Teapot is brighter but low from New York. The two grandest, [[dso:C80|Omega Centauri]] and [[dso:C106|47 Tucanae]], belong to the southern sky; both look like fuzzy stars to the naked eye.

steps.caption: M13 lies on the western side of the Keystone of Hercules, one third of the way from Eta down to Zeta Herculis. In binoculars it is a small round fuzzy 'star'.
Low in the summer south, toward the center of the galaxy, globular clusters crowd together. M22 is just up and to the left of the Teapot's lid; M4 sits beside Antares.
From Sydney, Omega Centauri rides high: the largest globular cluster of the Milky Way, with several million stars.

figures.caption: Open and globular clusters differ in every way: tens or hundreds versus hundreds of thousands of stars, young versus ancient, blue-white versus yellow. Switch to In the galaxy: they live in different places, too.

figures.caption: Globular clusters are balls of hundreds of thousands to millions of stars, so crowded at the centre that they merge into one glow. M13 is the finest for northern observers; Omega Centauri, the largest in our galaxy, is best seen from the southern hemisphere.

misconception.myth: A globular cluster is a young cluster that is still collapsing into a tight ball.
misconception.fact: Globular clusters are among the oldest things in the galaxy, around 11 to 13 billion years old. Their stars are held in a tight ball by their combined gravity, and have been for most of the universe’s history; it is the loose open clusters that are young.

check.prompt: Why do globular clusters look yellowish while young open clusters look blue-white?
choices: Their hot blue stars died billions of years ago
Dust in the halo makes them redder
They are moving away from us very fast
Their stars are made of different gases
check.explanation: Heavy blue stars live only millions of years. In a cluster 12 billion years old, only stars about as heavy as the Sun or lighter are left on the main sequence, plus orange giants, so the light is yellowish.

sections.heading: Clusters coming apart: the Big Dipper
body: Looser still are stellar associations and moving groups: stars born together that have spread too far apart to look like a cluster but still travel through space in the same direction at the same speed. The nearest is the Ursa Major moving group, only about 80 light-years away. Its core is the middle five stars of the Big Dipper: [[star:Merak|Merak]], [[star:Phecda|Phecda]], [[star:Megrez|Megrez]], [[star:Alioth|Alioth]] and [[star:Mizar|Mizar]]. The two end stars, [[star:Dubhe|Dubhe]] and [[star:Alkaid|Alkaid]], are unrelated and moving another way, so over tens of thousands of years the Dipper will slowly bend out of shape.

steps.caption: The five middle stars of the Big Dipper were born together and still move together. Dubhe and Alkaid, at the two ends, are not part of the group.

figures.caption: Five stars of the Big Dipper travel through space together; the two end stars are unrelated and head the other way. Run time forward or back 100,000 years and the familiar shape bends out of recognition.

check.prompt: Which Big Dipper stars do not belong to the Ursa Major moving group?
choices: Dubhe and Alkaid, the two end stars
Merak and Phecda, the bottom of the bowl
Mizar and Alioth, in the handle
None: all seven travel together
check.explanation: The middle five stars share the same motion through space; Dubhe at the end of the bowl and Alkaid at the end of the handle are moving another way.

sections.heading: Why clusters are the city observer's friend
body: Nebulae and galaxies are spread-out glows that city skyglow washes away. A cluster is made of stars, and points of light punch through light pollution far better. The Pleiades, the Hyades and the Beehive are large and bright enough that binoculars beat a telescope on them, even from Brooklyn. Globulars need more help: M13 is a fuzzy dot in binoculars, and it takes a telescope of about four inches or more to begin sprinkling it with individual stars.

figures.caption: Where to look: open clusters lie along the Milky Way band, because they live in the galaxy’s disc; globular clusters crowd towards the galaxy’s centre in Sagittarius, Scorpius and Ophiuchus, because they swarm around it in the halo.

sections.tryIt: Sweep binoculars slowly along the Milky Way through Cassiopeia and Perseus on an autumn evening. Every little knot of stars you stumble on is an open cluster.

keyPoints: Open clusters are young, loose groups of tens to thousands of stars in the Milky Way's disc.
Globular clusters are ancient, dense balls of hundreds of thousands of stars in the galaxy's halo.
Five Big Dipper stars form the core of the Ursa Major moving group, a family of stars drifting apart.
Clusters survive city skies better than nebulae and galaxies; many are at their best in binoculars.

questions.prompt: In a telescope you find a perfectly round ball of countless faint stars, blurring into a solid glow at the center. What is it most likely to be?
choices: An open cluster
A globular cluster
A planetary nebula
A moving group
questions.explanation: The round shape, huge star count and dense core mark a globular cluster. Open clusters are loose and irregular.

questions.prompt: Where in the galaxy do the two kinds of cluster live?
choices: Both kinds lie only in the disc
Open clusters in the halo, globular clusters in the disc
Open clusters in the disc, globular clusters in the halo around the center
Both kinds lie outside the Milky Way
questions.explanation: Open clusters form in the gas-rich disc, so they hug the Milky Way band. Globulars orbit in a sphere around the galactic center.

questions.prompt: Aldebaran sits at one tip of the V of the Hyades. What is its relationship to the cluster?
choices: It is a foreground star that happens to lie in the same direction
It is the cluster's brightest member
It is the star all the others orbit
It is a background star far behind the cluster
questions.explanation: Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, less than half the distance of the Hyades at about 150.

questions.prompt: How do astronomers know that five stars of the Big Dipper are related?
choices: They are exactly the same brightness
They are all the same color as the Sun
They are visibly orbiting each other
They share nearly the same distance, age and motion through space
questions.explanation: A moving group is identified by common motion and age. Dubhe and Alkaid move differently, so they are not members.

questions.prompt: Why do star clusters hold up better under city lights than galaxies do?
choices: Clusters are much closer than the Moon
Their light is concentrated in star points instead of a faint spread-out glow
City lights only block red light
Clusters are always overhead
questions.explanation: Skyglow drowns low-contrast glows first. Stars are concentrated points and stay visible against a bright background.

questions.prompt: Which statement about ages is correct?
choices: Open clusters are older than globular clusters
Both kinds are about as old as the Sun
Globular clusters are among the oldest things in the galaxy; open clusters are comparatively young
Cluster ages cannot be estimated
questions.explanation: Globulars are 11 to 13 billion years old. Open clusters like the Pleiades are around 100 million years old.
